newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Springsteen, alone, sings of ghosts and hard times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Springsteen, alone, sings of ghosts and hard times.

text.p: He looks more like a Dust Bowl folk singer than an exhilarating rocker whose concerts once turned a stadium into a giant party.
Bruce Springsteen is on the road again, armed with an acoustic guitar and a harmonica and singing about hard times, broken dreams and the struggles of people society left behind.

The inspiration for the new songs on the stark, spare "The Ghost of Tom Joad" album came from watching the John Ford film of John Steinbeck's "The Grapes of Wrath," Springsteen told the audience at a recent Fort Lauderdale concert.

"I wanted to do some work that will find its way into people's lives and maybe mean something. Tom Joad risked what he had for something that was bigger than he was," he said, referring to the protagonist in Steinbeck's classic novel of the Great Depression.

In going down his new path, Springsteen has done just that. Now aged 47, he has left behind the joyous, raucous days with his legendary E Street band, which peaked in popularity in the mid-1980s with "Born in the USA." But if his shows are less thrilling now, they are sobering and often deeply moving.

Sometimes bitter and sometimes wistful, Springsteen sings in "Straight Time" of an ex-convict tempted back into crime, in "The Line" of Mexican immigrants sneaking across the border at night and in "Galveston Bay" of the struggles between Vietnamese refugees and local fishermen on the Texas coast.

U.S. military veterans are also close to his heart. At Fort Lauderdale, he appealed to concert-goers to support the local veterans' association and he donated the profits from sales of tour merchandise to them.

In his new guise, "Born in the USA," a song about a veteran's return that Springsteen once had to tell President Ronald Reagan was not a patriotic anthem, is turned from the bombastic rock of the original into an anguished cry.

Other old songs are also given a new treatment. "Promised Land" was once a celebration of being young and heading out in the world. Now, in a slow, bluesy version, it is clear that Springsteen no longer believes in a promised land.
Springsteen rarely gives interviews but in lengthy preambles to songs at his concert here he offered some glimpses of his thinking.
"I knew myself really well when I was 23, which is evidence of how little I knew myself," he said, adding later: "Growing old is an uphill battle against cynicism."

In a hint of his thoughts on the glory days, he refers to "that 'Born in the USA' bulls---". Introducing "Straight Time" he said: "It's hard to step out to go to a place you've never been, even if your life depends on it."
A SPINNER OF WRY AND WITTY TALES

If the new "Boss" seems somewhat dour and serious these days, the three-hour show was far from an unbroken chronicle of misery. He is a born storyteller, spinning wry and witty tales in song introductions and cracking plenty of jokes.

A wealthy man, Springsteen is adored by his fans and respected by critics. After his divorce from model Julianne Philips he has been happily married for several years to his former back-up singer Patti Scialfa and has a young family.

But he is nonetheless convincing as a champion of the downtrodden. In October, he was made the first recipient of the "In the Souls of the People" award honouring Steinbeck from the San Jose State University's Steinbeck Research Centre. Presenting the award, Steinbeck's widow Elaine said the songwriter and the novelist both loved the same people.

And on stage this month, Springsteen told how moved he was by a scene in "The Grapes of Wrath" when Joad, having killed a man, must leave the family with which he has crossed America in search of a better life.
"When the world has dealt hard blows, people fall back on love, faith and family," he said. "Because ultimately that's all there is."
